The Oriental scops owl (Otus sunia) is a small, nocturnal predator widely distributed across Asia, from the Russian Far East through the Indian subcontinent to Southeast Asia. Newly hatched nestlings emerge from their eggs at a remarkably diminutive size, with a wet weight at birth of only 9.3 grams [Wwb = 9.3 grams]. This neonatal mass is typical for small strigiforms, reflecting the significant energetic investment required to produce a clutch. The incubation period, during which the female remains on the nest, is influenced by ambient temperature; at an incubation temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 24.5 days [ab = approximately 24.5 days], though field records indicate a broader range of 22 to 29 days depending on local microclimatic conditions. Soon after hatching, the nestling period begins, marking a phase of rapid mass gain and feather development. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, representing the very start of development, is 12.4 grams [Ww0 = 12.4 grams], a value that underscores the relatively large investment per offspring for a bird of this adult body size.

During the nestling phase, the altricial chicks are entirely dependent on parental provisioning, and their growth trajectory is steep. The time from hatching to the attainment of flight capability, or fledging, occurs at 25 days after hatching [tx = 25 days after hatching] under the active metabolic conditions typical of the species, when ambient temperatures reach 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Observed fledging times in the wild range from 18 to 26 days, with later dates often associated with cooler weather or reduced prey availability. Following fledging, the young birds enter a juvenile stage characterized by continued feather refinement and the development of hunting skills. The subsequent attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, is a critical life-history milestone, and for this species it occurs at 66 days since birth [tp = 66 days since birth] when maintained at the same active thermal regime of 40.2 °C at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively rapid maturation aligns with the species' semiannual breeding cycle and its occupation of seasonally productive habitats.

The first reproductive event marks a pivotal transition in the life cycle of the Oriental scops owl. Under the same warm conditions (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]) that characterize the active season, the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days], meaning that individuals generally delay their first breeding attempt until the second spring after hatching. This pattern of deferred reproduction is common among small owls, likely reflecting the need to establish a territory and attain sufficient body condition to support egg production. Regarding the annual reproductive output, females typically lay 3 to 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 5 eggs per clutch] and produce only one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year]. This modest fecundity is balanced by high parental investment, including extended brooding and consistent food delivery by both parents. The maximum reproductive rate is thus constrained by the single clutch, a strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity in a competitive environment.

In terms of overall longevity, the Oriental scops owl demonstrates a moderate lifespan for a bird of its size. Under the thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which approximate the body temperatures during active foraging and metabolic peaks, the maximum lifespan recorded is about 7.9 years [am = about 7.9 years]. This estimate, derived from mark-recapture studies and occasional captive records, indicates that individuals in the wild may survive for up to roughly 2,884 days, though the vast majority of mortality occurs in the first year after fledging. Adult survival rates are higher, with experienced breeders often returning to the same nest sites across multiple seasons. The species' metabolic machinery is finely tuned to its energetic needs; measurements of basal oxygen consumption, taken during the inactive phase under the same 40.2 °C thermal regime, yield a resting metabolic rate of 74.48 milliliters per hour [JOi = 74.48 milliliters per hour] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This value reflects the maintenance costs of a small endotherm.

Sexual size dimorphism is evident in the adult body masses of Otus sunia. The ultimate wet weight for females, representing the maximum recorded adult body mass, is 142 grams [Wwi = 142 grams], while males, which are generally more slender, attain an ultimate wet weight of 112 grams [Wwi = 112 grams]. This difference of roughly 30 grams is consistent with the reversed sexual size dimorphism seen in many raptors, where the larger female is thought to be better suited for incubating eggs and defending the nest against predators. The smaller male, meanwhile, benefits from greater agility during hunting, an advantage when provisioning the female and later the chicks. These adult masses represent the culmination of a rapid growth trajectory from the initial egg mass of 12.4 grams [Ww0 = 12.4 grams] through the nestling phase. Comparative data from related Asian Otus species suggest that such body masses are typical for this genus, correlating with their insectivorous diet and secondary dependence on small vertebrates in some populations.
